title: How to Spot a Phishing Page Before You Sign In
content:
A message says your account will be suspended unless you sign in now. The page has the right logo, your email address, and a familiar password box. Before entering anything, close that route and open the service independently. You can check a real account alert without trusting the page that delivered it.

The aim is to establish where you are sending credentials, not to grade a page's appearance. A polished copy can be fraudulent; an unfamiliar design can be legitimate. Use the following workflow before passwords, verification codes, or approval prompts become involved.

Start from a route you already trust

Open the service's installed app, use a bookmark you previously verified, or type its known address carefully. Avoid using the message's sign-in button, QR code, phone number, or “support” link to verify the message itself. A search result is another destination to check, not an automatic seal of legitimacy.

Google's phishing guidance advises going directly to the website when a message link asks for a password. Once there, check account notifications or the relevant order, document, or security setting. If you cannot confirm the request, contact the organization through an established channel.

Read the hostname, not the branding

Focus the address bar to see the full address. On a small screen, expand it rather than relying on a shortened display. Read the hostname: the part identifying the server, before the path and query. Words such as “login” or a company name elsewhere in the URL do not establish ownership.

The registrable domain combines a public suffix with the label immediately before it, as explained in Chromium's URL display guidance. Public suffixes can contain several labels, so “always read the last two words” is an unreliable rule. Establish the service's expected domain independently rather than guessing from a complicated address.

For example, in https://accounts.example.com/sign-in, the registrable domain is example.com. In https://example.com.sign-in.example.net/, it is example.net. The familiar text at the left does not change that. A path such as /example.com/login also cannot turn an unrelated host into the expected service.

Check spelling, extra hyphens, added words, and visually similar characters. Microsoft's typosquatting explanation describes substituted numbers and small spelling changes used to misdirect visitors. You do not need to solve every lookalike: if the address is difficult to establish, leave and use your trusted route.

Allow for legitimate sign-in redirects

A workplace portal may send you to a separate identity provider. A different domain therefore warrants verification, not an automatic accusation of phishing. Start from the organization's known portal and confirm unfamiliar sign-in destinations with its IT team. Do not approve an unexpected application-access request merely because the identity provider itself is genuine.

Understand what HTTPS does and does not establish

HTTPS protects the connection to the site named in the address bar. It does not establish that this site is the organization you intended to reach. An impostor can operate its own HTTPS site. A padlock or equivalent connection icon, copied logo, and professional layout cannot settle the identity question.

Chrome's connection-security guidance explicitly tells readers to check the site name even on secure connections. If the browser shows a dangerous-site or certificate warning, stop rather than bypassing it to sign in. Conversely, the absence of a warning does not prove a page is safe.

Use autofill as assistance, not a verdict

A password manager can reduce manual credential entry and associate saved credentials with websites. If it unexpectedly offers nothing, pause and recheck the destination instead of immediately copying your password into the page. But missing autofill alone does not prove phishing, and a credential suggestion alone does not certify the whole interaction.

Apple's AutoFill troubleshooting guidance notes that settings, unrecognized form fields, and website restrictions can prevent filling. Investigate those possibilities only after independently reaching the expected service. Avoid overriding a mismatch by editing a saved login's website to match an unverified page.

Know the protection passkeys provide

Microsoft explains that passkeys are associated with a specific service domain, preventing a lookalike domain from receiving the legitimate service's passkey authentication. This is stronger than trying to recognize every convincing imitation yourself.

NIST's authentication guidance describes WebAuthn phishing resistance through verifier-name binding. It also explains why manually entered one-time codes are not phishing-resistant: an impostor can relay them. Do not supply a code or approve a notification for a sign-in you did not initiate.

That protection has a scope. A passkey does not validate every document, payment request, or application permission shown after authentication. It does not resolve a compromised device or every account-recovery weakness. If a suspicious page asks you to abandon a passkey and type a password instead, return to the independently opened service before considering another method.

A hypothetical request, handled safely

Hypothetical example: Lina receives a shared-document alert naming her employer. The link opens https://work.example.com.review.example.net/ with an HTTPS connection and familiar branding. Her password manager offers no login. Those observations justify a pause, but the decisive next step is independent navigation.

She closes the tab, opens her established workplace portal, and checks for the document there. If it is absent, she contacts the sender through an existing conversation or asks IT to verify it. She does not return to the suspicious page to experiment with credentials. This is an illustrative scenario, not a reported incident or test result.

Exit first; recover through a trusted device if needed

If you entered nothing, close the suspicious tab and report the message through the service's reporting controls or your organization's established channel. Do not download its proposed fix or continue chatting with its “support” contact. If you typed a secret, treat it as potentially exposed even without pressing Submit.

From a trusted device, open the service directly. Follow its official recovery flow if locked out; otherwise change the exposed password and any reused copies. Google's compromised-account instructions also cover reviewing security events, recovery information, connected access, and suspicious account changes. For workplace accounts, notify IT promptly.

Review sessions and revoke unfamiliar access using the provider's controls rather than assuming a password change ends every session. Google's device-access guide explains reviewing devices and signing out sessions, while warning that unfamiliar names or locations can have legitimate explanations. Check unexpected authentication methods and email forwarding rules too.

Your check before signing in

  • Did I reach this service independently?
  • Does the full hostname match the service or a verified identity provider?
  • Is the action expected, without a browser security warning?
  • Am I avoiding manual overrides of unexplained credential mismatches?
  • Did I initiate any code request or approval prompt myself?
  • If uncertain, can I stop and verify without using the suspicious page?
excerpt: Check sign-in destinations independently, read domains carefully, understand HTTPS and passkey limits, and recover safely if credentials were exposed.
seoTitle: How to Spot a Phishing Page Before You Sign In
seoDescription: Check a sign-in page before entering credentials: navigate independently, inspect domains, understand autofill and passkeys, and recover account access safely.
